Open-plan offices were introduced with great promise. The idea was that removing walls would encourage collaboration, spark creativity, and reduce costs. However, the evidence suggests that the reality is more complicated.

Proponents point out that open layouts make it easy for colleagues to ask quick questions and share ideas. They also use space more efficiently, which can lower real estate expenses. For teams that rely on constant communication, these advantages can be significant.

On the other hand, open-plan offices come with notable drawbacks. Noise and visual distractions make it difficult to concentrate, particularly for tasks that require deep focus. Research has found that employees in open offices often interact less face to face, as they retreat behind headphones to create privacy. Many also report higher stress levels and more sick days.

The best approach is likely a balanced one. Offices that combine open collaborative areas with quiet zones, private rooms, and flexible seating allow people to choose the environment that fits their work. A well-designed workplace should support both teamwork and concentration rather than forcing a choice between them.
